doom.driver: Pentagon races to buy 10X more missiles as Iran war dwindles arsenal, threatens readiness for China aggression.
doom.blurb: WINNING THE WAR, LOSING THE NEXT ONE
doom.summary: The Pentagon is scrambling to quadruple interceptor purchases after the Iran conflict quietly hollowed out America's missile stocks — which is a deeply uncomfortable thing to discover *after* the shooting starts. Meanwhile, Trump is pivoting back to Iran sanctions as Hormuz talks stall, oil is back above $84, and the President apparently needed a catering truck to safely board a plane, which is either reassuring (great tradecraft) or terrifying (it came to that). North Korean missiles are now confirmed flying over Ukraine, Wall Street just handed Nvidia $500 billion for more AI chips, and somewhere in all this Colombia just had its worst earthquake in years. A busy, messy, multi-front Tuesday.

factors.name: Geopolitics
factors.detail: Iran deadlock deepens, Hormuz still closed, North Korean missiles confirmed in Ukraine, and the Pentagon's interceptor shortage is now officially a crisis — all in the same news cycle.

factors.name: Governance
factors.detail: Trump signs order splitting MMR vaccines against pediatric medicine consensus, while Senate's all-night SAVE America Act session collapsed in chaos — governance dysfunction on multiple fronts.

factors.name: AI Capability
factors.detail: Wall Street hands Nvidia $500 billion for AI data centers and Meta relaunches open-model strategy, accelerating capability buildout with limited new governance guardrails.

factors.name: Alignment
factors.detail: Zuckerberg's 6,500-word AI manifesto is more ideology than safety framework, but no acute alignment-failure headlines today.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: A magnitude 7.4 earthquake kills 132+ in Colombia with 2,700 still missing, adding a major humanitarian crisis to an already overloaded global crisis-response system.

doom.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing — ground-level view pressed flat against cracked concrete looking steeply upward inside a massive military depot warehouse, deep navy and smoldering orange palette, smoke-filtered light, heavy shadows dominating — the camera angle is almost floor-level, staring up at towering empty steel missile storage racks that stretch impossibly high toward a corrugated metal ceiling lost in shadow, the racks are modular green military shelving systems designed to cradle PAC-3 canister tubes, but the cradles are bare, their foam-lined mounting brackets hanging open and vacant, orange hazard striping on the rack edges catches the only warm light bleeding in from a distant loading bay door cracked open at ground level, casting a long thin smoldering rectangle of orange across the concrete floor that recedes toward the viewer, dust motes hang frozen in the beam, a single forgotten green canister end-cap lies discarded on the floor near the base of the nearest rack, the ceiling-mounted fluorescent strips overhead are half-dead, flickering cool blue-white against the dominant navy darkness, a forklift sits idle and abandoned mid-aisle, its forks lowered, casting a jagged shadow upward across the empty shelving, the sheer vertical emptiness of the racks towers over everything, conveying depletion and industrial-scale absence rather than arsenal, the atmosphere is airless, bureaucratic, and deeply unsettling.

dawn.driver: New train service connects Finland and Sweden for first time in decades. The service will enable rail travel from Portugal to Lapland - what is believed to be the longest train journey in Europe.
dawn.blurb: CONTINENT REUNITED BY RAIL, PORTUGAL TO LAPLAND
dawn.summary: In a world where new defence pacts and missile strikes dominate the headlines, Europe quietly stitched itself back together with steel and schedule. A restored Finland-Sweden rail link now makes it possible to travel by train from the sun-warmed coast of Portugal all the way to the Arctic edge of Lapland — what may be the longest continuous rail journey on Earth. It's a reminder that even as geopolitical fault lines deepen, nations can still choose to connect rather than divide, moving people and goods across a continent by the oldest, cleanest, most civilised means we know.

factors.name: Cooperation
factors.detail: Multiple European nations coordinating rail infrastructure to create an unbroken transcontinental route is a quiet triumph of political will and shared investment.

factors.name: Environment
factors.detail: Expanding rail networks provides a genuine low-carbon alternative to short-haul flights across Europe, a meaningful structural win for emissions reduction.

factors.name: Science
factors.detail: NASA's 'Big Bang' operation on Voyager 2 — squeezing more power from a 49-year-old spacecraft — showcases human ingenuity extending the reach of discovery.

factors.name: Human Spirit
factors.detail: Against a backdrop of earthquake devastation in Colombia, thousands of volunteers formed human chains to pass rubble — ordinary people choosing solidarity without being asked.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: A new GLP-1 pill delivering 12% weight loss in 36 weeks inches life-changing obesity medicine closer to the billions who cannot access or tolerate injections.

dawn.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing. Interior scene, we are seated inside the upper deck of a red and white VR double-decker Finnish passenger train the morning after its historic first crossing, looking out through the tall rectangular window at the aftermath scene outside. The train sits still at a modest northern platform, predawn transitioning to pale arctic gold on the horizon, the wide steel-grey Torne River visible in the distance catching the first amber light. Outside the window, the Haparanda platform is quiet now, intimate aftermath calm: a single forgotten Swedish blue-and-yellow flag lying on the frost-edged platform edge, two discarded coffee cups steaming faintly in the cold air, a station worker in a high-visibility jacket slowly sweeping confetti from the platform tiles. The window glass itself is faintly fogged at the corners from the warm train interior, the inside of the carriage glowing deep amber-gold from overhead lights contrasting against the cold teal-blue dawn outside. Far on the horizon through the glass, the flat subarctic landscape stretches in deep teal shadow, a thin radiant line of molten amber cresting the treeline. The dual rail gauges are visible at the platform edge, two sets of tracks side by side, one wider than the other, catching golden sidelight, long shadows stretching across the platform in the low Nordic dawn.
